items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how controllers in public healthcare envision human–AI collaboration in management control when dealing with uncertainty, complexity and equivocality, focusing on anticipated advantages and implementation challenges in an early-adoption setting. Design/methodology/approach We conducted an exploratory qualitative study with 14 controllers from Italian public healthcare organisations. Four closed-ended questions provided a preliminary picture of current AI adoption, while three scenario-based open-ended questions elicited prospective assessments. The framework method was used to analyse the data. Findings AI adoption remains limited and uneven, and is rarely embedded in everyday management control. Under uncertainty, controllers link AI to better forecasting and faster access to information, but worry about data quality, privacy and overreliance. In complex settings, they expect AI to help integrate diverse information and enable more systemic control, provided processes are standardised and human oversight remains. In equivocal situations, AI may support interpretation and communication, but its impact is limited by limited hands-on experience and the difficulty of codifying contextual nuances. Originality/value Based on the Jarrahi (2018) decision-making scenarios, the study develops a tentative conceptualisation of how public healthcare controllers envisage AI collaboration. The concerns of the participants inform three proposed arrangements: validation, recursive integration and contestable sensemaking. Their formulation and the accountability-augmentation principle are theoretical elaborations informed by prospective evidence and accountability research.

items.abstract_text: Purpose Agentic AI systems execute procurement decisions, reroute shipments and renegotiate supplier contracts at speeds that preclude real-time human review. The existing literature offers limited analytical attention to the risks that arise when decision authority is delegated to agents. This paper develops a risk taxonomy for agentic AI in supply chains and traces the hierarchical dependencies and influence magnitudes among the identified risks. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of literature, analyzed through theories–characteristics–contexts–methods framework, produces the risk taxonomy. A hybrid modified total interpretive structural modeling and fuzzy decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory methodology is then applied to structured expert judgments to establish the causal hierarchy and quantify inter-risk influence. Findings Three risks, namely workforce skill gap, data quality and reliability and ethical misalignment occupy the deepest level of the causal hierarchy. Lack of accountability and governance and data privacy emerge as terminal outcomes. All three analytical methods converge on a conclusion: agentic AI risks originate at the institutional layer, with technical risks acting as transmission mechanisms. Practical implications The findings indicate that effective governance requires that workforce capability, data integrity and objective-function alignment are addressed before deployment. The stratified agentic AI governance framework is proposed that translates hierarchical structure into a sequenced intervention architecture, providing practitioners with governance priorities organized by risk-propagation logic. Originality/value This paper contributes a systematically derived risk taxonomy and a causally weighted governance map for agentic AI risks in supply chains. Five propositions are derived from the causal structure and are advanced as a testable research agenda.

items.abstract_text: Purpose As artificial intelligence advances and its application scenarios continue to expand, human–artificial intelligence interaction grows increasingly close. While artificial intelligence brings convenience, it also raises concerns that it may weaken users' cognitive autonomy. To investigate this issue. This study aims to explore the composition of AI dependence and its impact on cognitive autonomy and specific aspects of creative performance. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on cognitive evaluation theory and the elaboration likelihood model to construct a dual-pathway model with instrumental dependence and affective dependence as core variables. The model explains the formation mechanisms of the two types of artificial intelligence dependence and their differential effects on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily examines their potential role in the elaboration dimension of creative performance. A two-stage mixed-method design was employed to test the model. Findings Study 1 found that perceived trust mainly had a positive effect on instrumental dependence. Different dimensions of interactivity differentially affected affective dependence and cognitive autonomy. Mediation analysis further confirmed the core mediating role of Dependence. Study 2, a small-sample exploratory experiment, re-tested selected hypotheses and found a possible negative effect of instrumental dependence on the elaboration dimension of creative performance. Research limitations/implications The main theoretical contribution of this study lies in revealing the dual-pathway formation mechanisms of artificial intelligence dependence and the reshaping effects of different types of dependence on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily explores the potential effects of dependence on elaboration performance. Originality/value The dual-pathway dependence model constructed in this study offers practical implications for understanding how long-term use of artificial intelligence affects cognitive autonomy.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how knowledge workers make sense of GenAI-enabled co-production, with particular attention to authorship ambiguity and its implications for competence attribution, self-evaluation and meaningful work. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a qualitative approach based on in-depth interviews with 32 knowledge workers who work directly with GenAI tools, combining inductive coding with abductive interpretation. We used the Gioia methodology to analyze participants' reported experiences and interpretations of human–AI collaboration, with sensemaking informing the interpretation of emergent themes and aggregate dimensions. Findings The findings identify authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. When GenAI contributes to ideation, analysis, drafting, coding or other knowledge-intensive outputs, workers may find it difficult to distinguish their own contribution from that of the technology. Participants responded to this ambiguity differently. Some reconstructed their expertise around judgment, validation and contextualization and experienced GenAI as extending their professional capability. Others struggled to internalize successful outputs as evidence of their own competence and reported impostor-like experiences and reduced meaningfulness. The findings suggest that experiences of GenAI-enabled co-production depend on whether workers interpret and reconstruct their contribution. Practical implications Managers in comparable knowledge-intensive settings may consider making human judgment visible, clarifying legitimate uses of GenAI and recognizing contributions beyond output speed and quality. Originality/value This study identifies authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. It shows how uncertainty regarding the respective contributions of the worker and GenAI can complicate competence attribution and initiate sensemaking about professional contribution. By explaining how workers' interpretations of authorship ambiguity are associated with divergent identity and meaning outcomes, including enhanced capability, impostor-like experiences and changing meaningfulness, the study extends research on human–AI collaboration beyond its predominant focus on performance and productivity.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This paper extends Luhmann's concept of programmes – decision premises specifying the conditions under which a system's binary code is operatively assigned – into the domain of algorithmically mediated communication. It conceptualises recommendation systems, ranking algorithms and feedback architectures as ambient cognitive programmes: recursive, probabilistic selectors that perturb the structural coupling between social and psychic systems, and examines the constitutional implications of their opacity and transfunctional reach. Design/methodology/approach The study develops a systemic–cybernetic model grounded in Luhmann's social systems theory and the epistemology of autopoietic cognition, integrating Teubner's theory of societal constitutionalism to address the normative dimensions of algorithmic mediation. Analytical illustrations from Facebook and TikTok contrast two recommendation architectures – affinity-based cascading and behavioural-similarity propagation – to demonstrate how the model applies across distinct platform logics. Findings Algorithmic cognitive programmes operate as meta-programmes that reconfigure multiple forms of social differentiation simultaneously, enacting a binary operational distinction of visibility/invisibility through engagement metrics. Their colonisation of communicative environments – by economic imperatives and, as the analysis argues, by the autonomous logic of technical mediation – becomes a constitutional pathology where its effects cannot be contested or corrected, requiring internal self-limiting mechanisms that render operative selection criteria observable to affected systems. Originality/value The paper advances a novel theoretical category – ambient cognitive programmes – that extends Luhmann's organisational typology by identifying a configuration it does not explicitly address: a purpose programme without a terminal goal state that continuously revises the conditional programmes it governs. It connects this analytical framework to Teubner's societal constitutionalism, proposing constitutional observability as a structural condition for the compatibility between algorithmic regimes and communicative pluralism.

items.abstract_text: Silicon Lifecycle Management (SLM) is essential for ensuring the reliability, security, and performance of modern computing platforms. Conventional SLM approaches rely on off-chip or software-only analytics, which lack on-die interpretability. We present X-OCTANE, an explainable on-chip telemetry-based anomaly notification engine. X–OCTANE is a hybrid explainability framework that integrates Causal-Preserving Mutual Information (CP–MI) with SHAP-based feature attribution for interpretable feature ranking and selection. The proposed feature rank-and-selection procedure retains competitive safety-oriented anomaly detection and bolsters security-specific in-field monitoring of compute platforms. For the 7 nm ASAP technology, X-OCTANE achieves competitive anomaly detection performance with less than 0.50% CPU die area and 1.0% non-idle power overhead. In addition, X–OCTANE improves anomaly-driven diagnosis accuracy by over 7% on average. Experimental validation using the PAMPAR benchmark suite on two separate experimental platforms demonstrates enhanced anomaly detection and diagnosis through the proposed explainable feature-rank-and-selection method. X–OCTANE establishes a scalable and transparent foundation for on-chip SLM analytics, unifying detection fidelity with causal interpretability.

items.title: AI-driven approaches for food risk assessment: current advances and future trends

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a tool to support food risk assessment and broader food safety activities in response to the growing complexity of global food supply chains, emerging foodborne hazards, and evolving food fraud practices. Unlike previous reviews that have largely focused on individual AI technologies or specific applications, this review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), transformer-based models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), multimodal learning, and emerging AI paradigms within a unified framework relevant to food risk assessment and food safety decision-making. The review examines their applications in hazard identification, contamination detection, predictive microbiology, risk classification, food fraud detection, surveillance, traceability, and decision-support systems. Particular attention is given to the strengths, limitations, interpretability, validation requirements, and implementation challenges associated with different AI approaches. The integration of AI with multimodal data sources, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, spectroscopy, biosensors, and advanced analytical platforms is also discussed as a means to improve risk prediction, monitoring, and early-warning capabilities. Key challenges include data quality and availability, model generalizability, limited external validation, computational requirements, interpretability, and regulatory acceptance. Emerging developments, including foundation models, federated learning, blockchain, digital twins, edge AI, and multimodal frameworks, are highlighted as promising directions for future research. Overall, this review provides a critical comparative framework for understanding the evolving role of AI in food risk assessment and related food safety applications, while identifying key scientific, technical, and regulatory priorities for future development and implementation. publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affective regulation, transfer, stable self-efficacy, persistence, and learning habits was much thinner. Ethical evaluation likewise remained uneven, emphasizing feedback quality, pedagogical validity, well-being, autonomy, motivation, inclusivity, and agency, while transparency, data minimization, scaffold fading, developmental suitability, manipulation risk, and ethical nudging were addressed far less often. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

items.abstract_text: This study employed a descriptive survey to investigate Yarmouk University students’ perceptions of AI as a tool for enhancing five specific EI skills. A self-administered questionnaire comprising 25 items was completed by a convenience sample of 384 students across five domains: AI’s role in stimulating motivation, developing social skills, developing self-awareness, developing empathy, and developing self-regulation. Both validity and reliability were established. Findings indicate that students perceived AI as moderately useful across all domains (overall M = 2.83, SD = 0.63). Statistically significant differences at α = 0.05 were found in all five domains based on gender, favoring males, though effect sizes were small (partial η² = 0.01-0.03). No statistically significant differences were found by college type. Although a significant multivariate effect emerged for academic level, none of the individual EI domains showed a statistically significant univariate difference. The results suggest that AI has emerged as a supplementary tool for developing aspects of EI among students, though its perceived effectiveness remains moderate. Implications for integrating AI into higher education to support emotional development.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) companions are increasingly used by post-secondary students for emotional support, stress management, and self-management, yet their potential implications for primary care in this population remain unclear. Students may engage with AI companions before encountering purpose-built therapeutic chatbots, which are more often accessed through intentional health-seeking or professional guidance. This distinction may position AI companions as an earlier influence on self-management and subsequent help-seeking. Objective: To examine how artificial intelligence (AI) companions may influence stress regulation, sleep quality, symptom interpretation, and healthcare-seeking behaviour among post-secondary students, and to identify the principal benefits, risks, and unresolved questions relevant to primary care. Methods: A conceptual narrative review was undertaken using literature identified through Harvard University’s Hollis Library and Google Scholar. Evidence related to AI companions, academic stress, sleep quality, emotional support, healthcare-seeking behaviour, primary care, and digital mental health was synthesized using Stress & Coping Theory and the stress-buffering hypothesis as theoretical foundations. Results: AI companions may support stress appraisal, cognitive reframing, emotional reflection, symptom articulation, and self-management before clinical encounters. However, they may also contribute to emotional overreliance, misinformation, reassurance seeking, sleep disruption, and altered help-seeking behaviour. This review proposes conceptual mechanisms linking AI companion engagement with stress regulation, sleep, and pathways into primary care while identifying relational intensity as a clinically meaningful dimension of engagement beyond frequency alone. Conclusion: AI companions should be understood as adjunctive rather than substitutive support. Their clinical relevance is based on how they can shape patients’ experiences before obtaining primary care. Longitudinal research is needed to determine how patterns of engagement influence stress, sleep, and healthcare utilization over time.

items.title: Does Graph Structure Improve AI-Generated Text Detection? A Controlled Audit with Tuned Baselines

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Graph neural network (GNN) detectors of AI-generated text report state-of-the-art accuracy, and the architectural claim that graph topology captures signals invisible to sequential classifiers is now common in the literature. We report the complete lifecycle of one such detector, from construction to falsification. AEGIS, a graph attention network over k-nearest-neighbour text graphs with multi-signal edge weights, reaches 98.50% accuracy on scientific abstracts with only 73K trainable parameters, outperforming five established baselines. We then subject our own system to the evaluation its headline number deserves: generation-time length control, format normalization, leakage-free splits, a tuned frozen-embedding probe as the calibrated null, and a 10 × 10 cross-generator transfer study over three seeds. Under this protocol the graph's apparent contribution collapses from +0.240 AUROC over a surface baseline to −0.0004 AUROC against the tuned probe, inside the measured replication noise floor, and the two detectors' transfer geographies are near-identical (ρ = 0.986). A single untuned regularization default manufactured a +0.027 phantom advantage. The structural differences the graph encodes are real, but they are a re-encoding of information already present in the embeddings. We distil the audit into a practical checklist for evaluating architectural claims in text detection, and argue that accuracy numbers and mechanism claims must be validated separately.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has made remarkable progress in pixel and text domains, yet human sketches a uniquely sparse and sequential data modality remain largely unexplored from an interpretability perspective. The recently proposed SketchXAI framework introduced Stroke Location Inversion (SLI) to reconstruct stroke layouts from randomized configurations, but treats every stroke with identical optimization priority regardless of its structural relevance. We address this limitation by proposing Attention-Guided Stroke Location Inversion (AG-SLI). We initially evaluate a continuous formulation that scales per stroke gradients proportionally to self attention weights across a 30-category QuickDraw subset (86.13% classifier accuracy). Through a staged empirical protocol, we demonstrate that this continuous variant fails to replicate consistently, exhibiting sign-flipping median convergence speed changes (−47.8% to +40.0%) driven by localized sampling noise. Motivated by this instability, we introduce a refined, bounded, rank-based formulation: a fixed multiplicative gradient boost is restricted to the top 30% most attended strokes across the final four transformer layers, decaying linearly over the optimization trajectory. Benchmarked against standard machine learning optimizers across independent hard-case pools (n = 90), the refined mechanism achieves a median convergence depth of 10 iterations, significantly outperforming standard Adam (19 iterations) and SGD with Momentum (24 iterations). Furthermore, the framework limits non-convergence rates to 22.2%, improves spatial recovery (0.038 Final MSE), and yields a net 30.65% reduction in total job wall-clock time despite an updated O(N log N) per step complexity. We present this complete empirical journey including the initial non replication to establish a transparent baseline for reproducible, resource efficient optimization architectures in sparse visual domains.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background : The concurrent occurrence of AI-induced disruption, rapid post-pandemic digitalization, and macroeconomic instability has fundamentally reshaped the psychological demands of modern work, creating a polycrisis. Staff members in digital work environments experience rising AI anxiety, digital overload, and technostress, but how such polycrisis-related demands impact PWB through these mechanisms and the extent to which personal resources may act as a shield against such an effect has not been comprehensively understood yet. Based on the assumptions of the Job Demands-Resources model, the present study examines a model of moderated mediation, wherein emotional exhaustion mediates the demand-PWB association, and psychological capital (PsyCap) moderates and strengthens PWB. Methods: Cross-sectional surveys using six psychometric scales were conducted among 340 full-time workers from sectors such as IT, Health care, Education, and Banking/Finance. Hypotheses regarding the structure were validated using CB-SEM with 5,000 bias corrected bootstraps whereas sector-specific MGA and fsQCA identified configurations related to lower PWB. Results: All three job demands were able to predict emotional exhaustion: AI anxiety (β = 0.396, p < 0.001), digital overload (β = 0.333, p < 0.001), and technostress (β = 0.318, p < 0.001), explaining 32.1% of the variance. Emotional exhaustion fully mediated the influence of all three variables on PWB (β = -0.434, p < 0.001) through bootstrapped indirect effects. PsyCap had a significant direct effect on PWB (β = 0.460, p < 0.001) for all four sectors. Through MGA, sector-specific differences emerged with regard to AI anxiety, which was more important in the IT sector, digital overload in Healthcare and Banking/Finance, and technostress in the Education sector. In fsQCA, digital overload was found as a necessary condition for low PWB (consistency = 0.909), where there were three configurations, each required low PsyCap as a boundary condition (solution consistency = 0.841, coverage = 0.573). Conclusions: Demands resulting from polycrisis are linked to low PWB mainly because of emotional exhaustion, and demand salience differs significantly across sectors. Low PsyCap functions as a universal boundary condition for low levels of well-being. Organisations should prioritise PsyCap development as an industry-invariant approach in addition to demand management, which takes into account the characteristics of the job.

items.title: Multidimensional AI Literacy and Students’ Acceptance of AI-Enabled Learning Technologies: A Higher-Order Extension of the Technology Acceptance Model

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract AI-enabled learning technologies are becoming routine in higher education. However, acceptance research tends to explain adoption through beliefs about technology while paying less attention to the capabilities that learners bring to AI interaction. Although AI literacy has recently been linked to acceptance, it is often modeled as a global score or as separate dimensions, leaving unresolved whether related competencies operate collectively within the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) mechanism. This study tests a higher-order extension of the TAM using survey data from 528 students across three Indonesian universities who had prior experience with AI for learning. AI literacy was specified through awareness, usage skills, critical understanding, and ethics awareness and estimated using a disjoint two-stage partial least squares structural equation modeling procedure. The results support a coherent higher-order representation and show that AI literacy is most strongly associated with perceived ease of use and is also positively related to perceived usefulness and attitude. Within TAM, attitude shows a stronger direct relationship with behavioral intention than usefulness. These findings position AI literacy as a learner capability layer that complements technology beliefs in explaining students’ evaluations of AI-enabled learning technologies. The study contributes a measurement-to-mechanism perspective that maintains practical, critical, and ethical competence in acceptance research and suggests that implementation should consider learner capability alongside access and usability. Because the evidence is cross-sectional, self-reported, and multi-tool, the relationships should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Natural language processing and AI models are increasingly used to extract emotional signals from textual data; however, systematic validation of different computational paradigms in emotionally complex relational contexts remains limited. Such approaches may contribute to digital health research, particularly in the fields of digital mental health and couples therapy, where understanding emotional expressions within romantic relationships is especially relevant. Objective This study aimed to compare a lexicon-based approach (NRC Emotion Lexicon) and a transformer-based model (Pysentimiento) in detecting affective patterns within spontaneous romantic relationship narratives and to evaluate their criterion-related associations with a theory-driven measure of relational well-being. Methods In this cross-sectional exploratory study, 112 Spanish adults completed the Couple Flourishing Measure (CFM) and provided an open-ended description of their romantic relationship. Narratives were analyzed using both computational approaches to generate emotion and sentiment indices. Pearson correlations were computed between model outputs and CFM scores. Steiger Z tests were conducted to compare dependent correlations across models. Results Both approaches showed significant associations with couple flourishing, although the transformer-based model yielded stronger correlations for several affective dimensions, particularly positive sentiment ( r =0.66, 95% CI 0.54-0.76) and negative sentiment ( r =−0.74, 95% CI −0.82 to −0.65). The lexicon-based approach showed smaller associations, primarily for negative emotions. Steiger Z tests identified significant between-model differences for disgust ( P =.04), joy ( P =.01), sadness ( P =.004), surprise ( P =.03), and positive and negative sentiment (both P <.001), but not for anger or fear. Conclusions In this sample, Pysentimiento showed stronger associations with couple flourishing than the NRC Emotion Lexicon across several affective dimensions, although differences were not consistent across all categories. These findings support the value of theory-driven external criteria for evaluating computational emotion detection in relational narratives and underscore the importance of context-sensitive interpretation when applying AI tools in psychologically sensitive domains. These findings also highlight the potential relevance of computational emotion analysis for digital health research, particularly in digital mental health and couples therapy research, although further validation in clinical settings is needed before clinical implementation.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background AI is increasingly embedded in health care and digital health applications, shaping clinical processes as well as how patients access information and participate in care. Research on bias in medical AI has largely focused on technical and performance-related disparities. Less attention has been paid to how such biases may affect patients’ access, understanding, trust, and opportunities for meaningful involvement in care. Objective This scoping review aimed to map how studies of bias in medical AI describe patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment and the digital divide and to identify gaps across technical, social, structural, and patient-centered perspectives. Methods This scoping review followed JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute) methodology and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE and EBSCOHost databases were searched in August 2025 and supplemented by Google Scholar searches. Peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 onward were included if they addressed bias in medical AI and described patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment or digital inequality. Data charting focused on AI application types, bias dimensions, patient empowerment domains, digital divide–related factors, intersectionality, and debiasing strategies. Findings were synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results The search identified 497 records, of which 22 studies met the inclusion criteria. Bias was represented as a multidimensional sociotechnical phenomenon, with social bias identified most frequently (21/22 studies), followed by algorithmic bias (16/22 studies), structural bias (14/22 studies), and design-related bias (12/22 studies). Patient empowerment was most frequently addressed through involvement in care (n=13), followed by health literacy (n=9) and trust and assurance (n=7), whereas broader psychosocial and everyday-life domains were addressed less frequently. Digital divide–related factors were identified in 19 of the 22 studies, with digital literacy and usability barriers reported most frequently. Seven studies considered 2 or more social or structural dimensions of disadvantage. Although many studies discussed approaches that could mitigate bias-related barriers, explicit empirical evaluation of debiasing strategies in relation to patient empowerment or digital equity was largely absent. Conclusions Patient-related consequences of bias in medical AI extend beyond algorithmic performance and are reflected in access, understanding, trust, and involvement in care. Broader empowerment dimensions, multidimensional disadvantage, and empirically evaluated mitigation strategies remain comparatively underexplored.

items.abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a promising technology for supporting mathematical dialogue, feedback, and reasoning in mathematics education. However, research has paid limited attention to how university students’ geometric thinking develops through sustained interaction with GenAI, particularly in geometry transformation learning. This study aims to develop a Dialogic Geometric Thinking Framework that characterizes the dimensions and progression of university students’ geometric thinking during sustained dialogue with ChatGPT. A qualitative exploratory design was employed involving undergraduate mathematics education students enrolled in a Geometry Transformation course at an Indonesian public university. Data were collected from student–ChatGPT dialogue transcripts, students’ written solutions, and reflective interviews. The data were analyzed thematically using reflexive thematic analysis to identify recurring characteristics and relationships among dimensions of geometric thinking and to synthesize them into an integrated framework. The findings identified five interrelated dimensions of geometric thinking: conceptual reasoning, representational coordination, procedural justification, reflective regulation, and mathematical elaboration. These dimensions illustrate how students progressively articulate mathematical concepts, coordinate representations, justify solution procedures, evaluate their reasoning, and extend mathematical ideas during AI-mediated dialogue. The study resulted in a Dialogic Geometric Thinking Framework that provides a process-oriented perspective on the development of university students’ geometric thinking during interaction with GenAI. The framework offers an initial theoretical foundation for understanding and further investigating geometric thinking in AI-mediated mathematics learning. Keywords: geometric thinking, generative artificial intelligence, chatGPT, geometry transformation, mathematical dialogue.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of pupils' everyday lives and of school life. Written from the perspective of a primary school teacher and principal, this perspective paper examines three interrelated concerns of the author herself. These concerns arose from a wish to protect her pupils and led her to study the topic for her own professional development and to help her colleagues make teaching safer and better. They concern developing critical thinking towards AI-generated answers, protecting the personal data of minors, and the fear that excessive assistance from AI will weaken pupils' thinking. Drawing on a narrative, non-systematic review of recent research on cognitive offloading, the European and Greek regulatory framework, and illustrative examples from the author's own teaching practice and lesson scenarios for primary school, it argues that the fear of cognitive dependence is a plausible concern rather than an established finding for primary school pupils. The available evidence, which comes mainly from adolescents and adults, suggests that the form of AI support (whether it replaces the learner's effort or scaffolds it) may be an important factor. AI is regarded throughout as a valuable tool; the risk lies mainly in the way it is used. The classroom examples come from ordinary lessons whose only purpose was to teach pupils to question AI answers and to protect themselves when using AI. They were not planned as research, no research data were collected, and they are offered as the author's practitioner reflections, not as findings. The author's classroom experience illustrates that such activities can be implemented in ordinary primary school lessons, but their effects on pupils' critical thinking have not yet been evaluated. The paper relates the three concerns to long-standing educational principles, in particular Socratic questioning, Dewey's reflective thought and Vygotskian scaffolding. On this basis, it proposes a simple, as yet untested three-step classroom protocol (``think -- ask -- check''), age-appropriate data protection rules, and a role for school leadership, and outlines questions for future research.

items.title: Minds Meet Machines: The Joint Role of Trust and Intellectual Humility in AI Persuasion

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Research shows that AI models have a remarkable ability to change people’s minds following a short conversation, a notoriously difficult task for human communicators. Such persuasive paradigms provide a unique opportunity to examine which psychological characteristics predict receptivity to counter-attitudinal information. We focus on two characteristics: intellectual humility (IH), reflecting openness to revising one’s beliefs following new information, and trust in the information source (AI). To establish the role of a-priori dispositions that determine acceptance of new information, we ran two online studies, sampling British participants with a negative attitude toward legal immigrants (N = 294). We replicated previous findings showing significant and lasting attitude change following a brief exchange with GPT, but crucially, this effect was not uniform. In Study 1, attitude change was greatest among participants with higher initial trust in AIs and higher intellectual humility. Study 2 extended this finding by measuring both dispositions a week before the conversation with GPT, revealing the same pattern: opinion change was greatest among those who were both open to new information and trusting of its source. These findings highlight the centrality of recipient dispositions, suggesting that the relationship between source trust and persuasion depends on recipients' intellectual humility. More broadly, source trust may function as more than a heuristic cue, and its relationship with attitude change may depend on recipients' willingness to recognize the fallibility of their beliefs. Together, these findings extend perspectives on persuasion by highlighting the joint role of source trust and recipients' epistemic dispositions in belief revision.

items.abstract_text: Heart disease is one of the most common causes of death in the world and early identification of individuals at elevated cardiovascular risk requires reliable risk-assessment methods that can support clinical decision-making. Many conventional machine-learning models focus primarily on disease classification or risk prediction and do not explicitly provide patient-specific virtual representations. This study introduces CardioTwin-AI, a Digital Twin-based Adaptive Risk-Aware Learning Framework (ARLF) to predict the presence or absence of heart disease. We propose a data-driven, patient-specific Digital Twin representation based on clinical attributes, in which the patient state is mapped to a corresponding virtual state and evaluated using state-level synchronization measures, including Twin Simulation Error (TSE) and Twin Fidelity Score (TFS) to quantify representation consistency. The deep feature representations are generated by feature engineering process based on autoencoder, and then analysed by the ARLF prediction model to estimate the probability of the presence of heart disease. It achieved high patient-state representation consistency between the source clinical state and its virtual representation, with a Twin Fidelity Score of 99.76% and a Twin Simulation Error of 0.002402. The proposed ARLF model achieved accuracy of 90.21%, precision of 90.32%, recall of 94.11%, F1-score of 92.18%, and ROC-AUC of 95.13% in the fixed held-out evaluation. The results indicate the potential of CardioTwin-AI for predicting the presence or absence of heart disease and assessing patient-state representation consistency, subject to further external validation and prospective clinical evaluation.

items.abstract_text: The Research Topic begins with Achuthan's Artificial intelligence and learner autonomy: a meta-analysis of self-regulated and self-directed learning, which provides a broad empirical examination of the relationship between AI and learner autonomy. Synthesizing 32 empirical studies, 92 effect sizes, and 3,029 participants, the study examines the effects of AI-based interventions on SRL, self-directed learning (SDL), different dimensions and phases of SRL, and learning outcomes. The findings indicate positive effects of AI interventions on overall SRL and SDL, with particularly notable effects during the forethought phase, including goal setting and planning. At the same time, less consistent effects for behavioral regulation point to an important design challenge: supporting learners in knowing what to do and why to do it does not necessarily ensure that they will translate those intentions into effective action. The findings therefore provide encouraging evidence for AI as a scaffold for self-regulation while highlighting the importance of designing support across the full SRL cycle.Building on this macro-level evidence, Agustin's AI as a co-regulator: relational design for strengthening self-regulated learning addresses the theoretical mechanics of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in Winne and Hadwin's COPES architecture, this conceptual paper tackles a core dilemma in educational technology: how can AI assist learners without eroding the cognitive agency and productive struggle essential to self-regulation? Agustin introduces "productive metacognitive friction" -the deliberate structuring of challenge and discrepancy within AI interaction -as a design mechanism to prevent passive reliance. The article presents five relational design principles alongside an evaluation framework prioritizing learner autonomy, interpretability, process integrity, and long-term developmental growth across both formal education and workplace reskilling environments.Moving from meta-analytic synthesis and conceptual frameworks to empirical classroom research, Gu et al.'s Fostering feedback literacy by scaffolding self-regulated feedback: a comparative study of GenAI and human peers examines the operational mechanisms through which GenAI fosters feedback literacya key component of self-regulated learning. In a comparative mixed-methods study of first-year undergraduates in Hong Kong, the authors compare the developmental impact of GenAI-generated feedback against traditional human peer review. Their findings demonstrate that GenAI yields a statistically significant improvement in feedback literacy over human peer feedback alone. Qualitative evidence reveals that this advantage stems from GenAI's ability to scaffold distinct self-regulatory behaviors: providing immediate, non-judgmental spaces for goal setting, structured planning, critical evaluation, and real-time self-reflection. By removing the interpersonal friction and psychological safety concerns common in peer review, GenAI emerges as an effective tool for cultivating student feedback literacy.Finally, Chang et al.'s "Should I tell my teacher?" Student AI disclosure practices, stigma, and selfregulated learning in higher education examines the affective, social, and institutional factors that influence how learners adopt these tools in practice. Focusing on undergraduate students at a Canadian university, the authors explore the intersection of student AI disclosure practices, social stigma, and SRL processes. Their findings illuminate a key tension: while transparent disclosure to instructors correlates with proactive self-regulated learning behaviors (a "transparent-disclosure pattern"), fear of academic judgment and social stigmatization often triggers an "anxious-concealment pattern." Highly anxious students who use AI heavily are more likely to conceal their usage or restrict sharing to peer networks. This study highlights that technical scaffolds cannot succeed in a vacuum; institutional policies and pedagogical environments must account for emotional and social dynamics to prevent secrecy from undermining reflective SRL practices.Considered together, the four articles in this Research Topic illustrate that AI's role in self-regulated learning extends far beyond simple automation or content delivery. Achuthan's meta-analysis provides evidence of AI's potential to strengthen SRL and SDL, while also identifying limitations in behavioral regulation. Agustin's framework addresses this challenge conceptually by positioning AI as a co-regulator that supports learners without displacing their agency. Gu et al. demonstrate how such support can be enacted in feedback processes, whereas Chang et al. show how emotions, stigma, and institutional expectations shape learners' decisions about AI use. This collection highlights that realizing the promise of AI-supported self-regulated learning requires more than personalization or automation. Research and design must examine how AI can scaffold regulatory processes, support learner autonomy and human agency, and safeguard against cognitive over-reliance.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Watershed environmental governance increasingly combines dense sensing infrastructure with institutions whose attention, authority, and coordination capacity remain limited. We develop the cognitive orchestration layer as a theory-building concept for examining how large language model (LLM)-based agents may connect sensing, assessment, decision advice, institutional response, and feedback without displacing domain models or public authority. Methods The Agentic Framework for Watershed Governance (AFWG) specifies three enabling pathways, three institutional interfaces, and four propositions. A purposively selected set of eight publicly documented cases is used to illustrate functional configurations, source limitations, and research gaps; it is not a systematic review or empirical evaluation. Results The cases document sensing, assessment, and decision-support functions, but do not establish improved decision quality, sustained institutional use, environmental outcomes, or agent-executed response closure. MAESTRO is retained as an adjacent-domain design illustration, not an existence proof of full-loop closure: human authorization remains necessary, and its reported performance has not been independently replicated. Discussion Transfer to watershed governance is plausible only where domain models remain authoritative, outputs carry provenance and uncertainty, named officials retain authority to authorize consequential actions, and institutional audit and failure handling are built into deployment. AFWG therefore offers a bounded conceptual framework and a falsifiable research agenda, rather than a claim that agents have already closed the watershed response loop.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Artificial intelligence is transforming higher education and professional communication, creating a tension between technological automation and human critical thinking. In teaching communication, this tension highlights the need to rethink the skills students should develop as AI becomes increasingly integrated into academic and professional practice, especially the ability to use AI strategically without losing human judgment, ethical reasoning, and decision-making in their context. Methodology The study uses an exploratory-descriptive, cross-sectional, mixed-methods design combining quantitative and qualitative evidence to explore how students and program directors in Ecuador perceive AI integration in communication education. It surveyed 230 students across seven institutions and conducted 12 semi-structured interviews with directors. Survey analysis identified AI usage patterns, while thematic analysis of interviews focused on benefits, barriers, ethics, and priorities. Initially, Pearson's chi-square test examined associations with sociodemographics, but it was unreliable due to low expected cell counts. Findings are presented as descriptive patterns, not inferential or population-level conclusions. Results Students report using AI mainly for communication (28.70%), trend prediction and audience analysis (13.04%), and segmentation (9.57%). Four AI applications were identified: operational efficiency, strategic analysis, audience management, and digital optimization. The gender-based chi-square test was inconclusive ( χ 2 = 12.728; df = 14; p = 0.548), with over 50% of cells having fewer than 5 responses. Among directors and coordinators, common uses included content generation, assisted writing, research, data analysis, and audience engagement. The thematic analysis revealed four patterns: operational efficiency, decision-making, automation vs. human judgment, and training needs. Discussion and conclusions Communication students in Ecuador mainly use AI to improve efficiency and effectiveness, with key applications in trend prediction, audience analysis, and segmentation. Program leaders see AI as useful in content creation, research, and audience engagement. The study identifies four AI use areas: operational efficiency, strategic analysis, audience management, and digital optimization. The study highlights tension between automation and human judgment, stressing the continued importance of critical thinking, creativity, ethics, and context. It proposes a framework balancing AI automation with human input to support strategic communication decisions.

items.abstract_text: With the widespread adoption of online educational technologies, instructional videos have become a pivotal tool for flexible and efficient learning. The integration of visual aids, such as animations and dynamic elements, aims to enhance the learning experience; however, their effectiveness remains debated. This study examined learning performance and subjective experience when instructional videos presented static AI-generated images or manually animated versions of those images. A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 40 undergraduate participants ( n = 10 per cell), comparing static versus motion-enhanced presentation conditions across male and female participant groups. Stable Diffusion XL generated the base images, and CapCut was used to add motion; the motion itself was not AI-generated. Participants viewed a 140-s mobile video on mortise-and-tenon structures, completed a 10-item accuracy test, and rated willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and mental effort. The ANOVA results provided no statistically significant evidence of a main effect of motion on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several subjective outcomes. For acceptability, the gender × motion interaction was statistically significant, but Bonferroni-adjusted simple-effect tests supported a gender-group difference only in the static condition. For mental effort, the interaction was also statistically significant; adjusted simple-effect tests indicated higher mental effort among female than male participants in the dynamic condition and higher mental effort in the static than dynamic condition among male participants. Given the small sample and multiple outcomes, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

items.abstract_text: Background AI feedback holds promise for supporting student learning, but unstructured use can lead students to passively accept AI-generated answers, weakening their independent reasoning. This study examined whether structured AI feedback affects undergraduate students' critical thinking, learning performance, and engagement in a data science analytics course. Methods An exploratory two-class quasi-experimental study was conducted in a three-month undergraduate data science course ( N = 167). One class received four-phase structured AI feedback, while the comparison class received conventional instructor feedback. Propensity score matching was used to improve comparability on observed baseline characteristics. Critical thinking was assessed using an adapted 40-item assessment covering five dimensions. Results Students receiving structured AI feedback demonstrated higher post-test critical thinking scores than matched controls, with a baseline-adjusted difference of 5.64 points (95% CI [3.62, 7.65], p &lt; 0.001). A significant between-group difference in pre-to-post changes was also observed. Dimension-level analyses revealed significant differences in Evaluation of Arguments, Interpretation, Recognition of Assumptions, and Inference, while Deduction showed no significant difference. Higher learning performance, cognitive engagement, and behavioral engagement were also observed in the structured AI feedback group, whereas emotional engagement did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusion The findings provide exploratory evidence of differences in critical thinking and learning outcomes between the structured AI feedback and conventional instructor feedback classes. They highlight the potential relevance of feedback designs that encourage students to actively evaluate, question, and revise AI-supported analytical work, while underscoring the need for further studies that can isolate intervention-specific effects.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and self-regulated learning theory, this explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined an AI-supported motivated self-regulated learning framework using a cross-sectional survey of 486 university EFL students and follow-up interviews with 20 students. Structural equation modeling identified a positive direct association between reported AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement, together with a positive indirect statistical association through learning autonomy and self-regulated learning. Integration of the two strands highlighted variation in how learners evaluated and incorporated feedback. These self-report findings do not establish temporal ordering or causal effects. They identify learner agency, strategic regulation, and critical evaluation as relevant considerations for future investigations of AI-supported writing.

items.abstract_text: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics
items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded across the scientific research lifecycle, while prevailing governance remains centered on disclosure of tool use and the assignment of responsibility to human authors. We argue that disclosure is necessary but insufficient because it does not establish that researchers understood, verified, challenged, and authorized the AI-assisted processes that shaped scientific claims. We define this disconnect as the epistemic accountability gap and develop the Lifecycle Epistemic Accountability Framework (LEAF) as a testable theory of how meaningful human control can be preserved across AI-assisted knowledge production. Drawing on a structured integrative review and critical interpretive synthesis, LEAF links four human-control capacities—competence, contestability, intervention authority, and traceable ownership—supported by evaluability by design, to five lifecycle checkpoints spanning evidence identification, study design and ethics, data processing and analysis, interpretation, and reporting or knowledge translation. The framework proposes that accountability improves when oversight is exercised prospectively at epistemically consequential decision points, documented through an audit trail, and calibrated to epistemic materiality: the extent to which AI assistance can alter the validity, interpretation, or consequences of a scientific claim. Six propositions specify testable relationships among disclosure, epistemic materiality, meaningful human control, lifecycle checkpoints, auditability, and defensibility of scientific claims. LEAF therefore shifts AI research governance from retrospective visibility to prospective, risk-proportionate control. We identify boundary conditions, implementation pathways, and an empirical research agenda for testing the framework across disciplines and resource settings. LEAF's distinctive explanatory mechanism is conditional: epistemic materiality escalates oversight, evaluability enables four human capacities, lifecycle checkpoints interrupt error propagation, and retained audit evidence makes consequential decisions answerable.

items.abstract_text: Digital transformation is reshaping academic work through remote and hybrid arrangements, intensified digital connectivity and the expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI). These developments can support flexibility, autonomy and efficiency, but may also intensify workload, erode work–life boundaries and generate demands associated with continuous adaptation, academic integrity and professional responsibility. Existing evidence is fragmented across technostress, remote and hybrid work, digital readiness and AI-enabled academic work, leaving insufficiently explained how technological change becomes embedded in the organisation and experience of academic work and, through this process, relates to wellbeing. This conceptual paper addresses this gap by developing the Digital Academic Work Reconfiguration and Wellbeing (DAWR-W) Framework. The framework was developed through theory synthesis informed by a structured literature foundation of 40 empirical studies and complementary theoretical research. The synthesis distinguishes the characteristics through which digital transformation reconfigures the organisation, boundaries, demands, relationships and professional content of academic work from the psychosocial mechanisms through which academics experience these changes. The resulting framework identifies seven characteristics of digitally transformed academic work and six psychosocial mechanisms involving resource depletion and replenishment, recovery and psychological detachment, perceived control and autonomy, competence and adaptive capacity, relational connection and psychological safety, and professional meaning and identity. Organisational and institutional conditions shape how digital transformation becomes embedded in academic work, while boundary conditions and feedback processes recognise contextual variation and adaptation over time. The central contribution of the DAWR-W Framework is to position work reconfiguration, rather than technology exposure alone, as the occupational process connecting digital transformation with academic employee wellbeing. In doing so, the framework integrates previously fragmented digital-work phenomena within a common explanatory architecture and locates responsibility for sustainable digital academic work across both individual and institutional levels. It provides an occupation-specific foundation for empirical testing, work-design interventions, and digital and AI governance in higher education.

items.abstract_text: Purpose: The study aimed to investigate the feasibility of employing selected artificial intelligence (AI) software to generate contemporary textile designs. Focusing on bridging textile design and AI, with a methodological approach for the Ghanaian Textile Designer. With AI emerging as a transformative force in multiple industries, including textiles, the research sought to assess its capacity to enhance design processes and meet consumer preferences. Methodology/Design: Three AI software programs, including Playground, Leonardo, and Lexcia, were selected for the study. Each was provided with identical prompts to generate contemporary textile designs. The outputs were then systematically analysed to identify similarities, differences, and overall design quality. Findings: The results showed that while the software received identical prompts, the generated designs displayed notable variations, alongside some shared visual features. The AI-driven process proved significantly faster and more efficient than traditional methods and yielded designs consistent with consumer specifications. Practical and Social Implications: The findings suggest that AI tools can substantially improve productivity, creativity, and responsiveness in textile design. Introducing AI-based design tools to textile designers in Ghana could enhance competitiveness, foster innovation, and better align production with evolving market demands. Originality: This study offers an early exploration of the comparative application of multiple AI software tools for contemporary textile design, contributing novel insights into their feasibility, efficiency, and adaptability within the Ghanaian textile industry context.

items.abstract_text: Purpose: This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) driven talent management practices and the performance of agri based enterprises in the Central Region of Cameroon, focusing on the mediating roles of workforce productivity and employee resilience. Research Methodology: A quantitative cross sectional survey design was employed, targeting 250 managers and human resource professionals. Data were collected with a structured questionnaire and analyzed with SPSS and AMOS through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and mediation analysis with 5.000 bootstrap resamples. Results: AI driven talent management was positively and significantly related to enterprise performance (r=0.523, p<0.01). Workforce productivity (β=0.18) and employee resilience (β=0.14) significantly mediated this relationship. Both the total indirect effect (β=0.32, p<0.01) and the direct effect (β=0.29, p<0.01) were significant, indicating partial mediation, with about 52 percent of the total effect transmitted through the two mediators. Conclusions: AI driven talent management enhances the performance of agri based enterprises both directly and indirectly through improved workforce productivity and stronger employee resilience. Enterprises should integrate AI strategically into talent management and support employees through change management. Limitations: The cross sectional design, self reported data, purposive sampling, and focus on a single region limit causal inference and generalizability. Contributions: The study provides empirical evidence from an underresearched African agricultural context and clarifies the mechanisms through which AI driven talent management translates into enterprise performance.

items.abstract_text: As digital technology becomes more deeply embedded in education, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly present in junior high school students' daily learning. This paper explores the "scaffolding" role of GenAI in students' self-regulated learning (SRL) and its possible influence on enhancing academic self-efficacy. Based on Zimmerman's cyclical phase model of SRL and learning scaffolding theory, the study systematically deduces the human-AI interaction process. The analysis suggests that GenAI acts as planning, monitoring, and reflective feedback scaffolds across the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases, effectively addressing the lack of personalized support in traditional autonomous learning. Furthermore, GenAI assistance contributes to the internalization of academic self-efficacy by accumulating direct mastery experiences and alleviating trial-and-error anxiety. Acknowledging the potential risks of cognitive offloading and academic misconduct associated with GenAI dependency, the paper proposes coping strategies such as cultivating students' critical GenAI literacy and implementing dynamic scaffold fading. This research provides theoretical support and practical guidance for educators to optimize GenAI-assisted self-regulated learning environments.

items.abstract_text: Against the backdrop of generative AI emerging as a core strategic asset for major powers, the rhetorical tropes of national security and industrial competitiveness are subject to strategic manipulation by divergent domestic actors. The deregulatory camp within the White House invokes industrial competitiveness to roll back security-focused executive orders; the security faction in Congress expands chip export controls in the name of national defense; state-level authorities counter federal overreach through consumer protection mandates; and Silicon Valley deploys a two-pronged lobbying strategy. Taking the 2023-2026 policy pendulum and BIS chip regulations as its analytical case, this paper demonstrates that domestic contestation spills over globally through transmission channels. This has produced a global AI governance landscape defined by fragmentation, hollowed-out soft law processes, and a three-bloc divide across the U.S., the EU, and China, while the shortening commitment half-life of U.S. policy positions has inflated the costs of multilateral cooperation. The study also identifies limited positive spillover effects. In response, the paper puts forward targeted strategies. The conclusion argues that U.S. internal regulatory divisions constitute a mechanism that externalizes domestic political costs as global governance uncertainty. Understanding this mechanism is a prerequisite for reshaping the multilateral AI order.

items.abstract_text: With AI agents increasingly involved in teamwork, whether AI can substitute human collaboration has become a heated topic in academia. Large-model-driven agents are now capable of participating in team brainstorming, task coordination, and collaborative problem-solving, and knowledge-intensive industries are beginning to form a large number of human-machine hybrid teams. Existing research mostly relies on theoretical reasoning and lacks empirical perceptual data from front-line practitioners. Drawing on a questionnaire survey of 158 employees with cross-industry teamwork experience, this paper explores practitioners' perceptions regarding the substitution of human collaborative behaviors by AI. The results show that AI can only partially substitute procedural and rule-oriented collaborative tasks, whereas social-emotional communication, conflict mediation and value judgment remain irreplaceable human strengths. Position, work experience and AI familiarity jointly shape individual perceptions of the substitution boundary. Most practitioners regard AI as an auxiliary tool rather than a leader of team collaboration. This study provides a practical reference for enterprises applying AI collaboration tools.

items.venue: Journal of Education and Learning Reviews
items.abstract_text: Background and Aim: Evidence on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in secondary science education remains limited. This systematic review examined students’ conceptual understanding and engagement, teachers’ pedagogical strategies and challenges, and students’ critical thinking and scientific inquiry. Materials and Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, ERIC, Scopus, and Lens.org were searched for peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2022 and 2026. Two authors independently screened 187 unique records (Cohen’s κ = .78), identifying 20 eligible studies. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Framework synthesis integrated findings, informed by Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK). Results: Seven studies assessed AI capabilities rather than classroom implementation. Only two compared learning outcomes across conditions; none employed a randomized controlled design. Student perceptions and engagement were generally positive, whereas learning outcomes were mixed. A chatbot supporting self-regulated learning outperformed a rule-based chatbot, but ChatGPT-4o yielded smaller gains than peer collaboration. Teachers reported concerns regarding content accuracy, assessment reliability, and instructional readiness. Generative AI matched or exceeded student performance on structured examinations but demonstrated lower grading reliability than human assessors. Evidence concerning critical thinking was particularly limited. Richer reasoning was reported with dialogue-oriented tools or teacher guidance, whereas answer-seeking use of general-purpose tools was associated with weaker reasoning. Conclusion: Pedagogical structuring was recurrently associated with productive AI use, although causal inference remains limited. A provisional model warrants empirical testing. Priorities include structured tasks, science-specific teacher development, human assessment oversight, explicit AI literacy instruction, school governance, and controlled comparisons of structured and unstructured use across secondary science classrooms.

items.abstract_text: Cueing paradigms are commonly used to study the neural mechanisms of visual spatial attention control. quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in language education, yet evidence from secondary-school settings remains fragmented. This integrative review examines empirical research on GenAI in formal secondary language education published from January 2023 to September 2026, with attention to pedagogical applications, language skills and activities, learning outcomes, teacher mediation, implementation challenges, and gaps in the evidence. quarantine.abstract_text: With the growing adoption of generative AI (GenAI) in higher education, concerns have emerged about excessive AI dependence and the inappropriate use of AI-generated content. However, few studies have examined the relationships among AI dependency (AID), cognitive offloading (CO), and AI-giarism (AIG). These findings indicate that AID is associated with self-reported AIG both directly and indirectly through CO within the specified model. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish causal relationships, and the self-reported outcome does not confirm actual incidents of academic misconduct. These findings highlight the importance of teacher education approaches that promote responsible AI use, independent reasoning, critical evaluation of AI-generated information, and transparent disclosure of AI assistance.

quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction Adolescents increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots for schoolwork, yet evidence on whether this use supports or undermines learning is mixed. quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Lexical errors are among the most frequent and persistent issues in second language (L2) production, yet research on vocabulary exercises has largely focused on the acquisition of new words rather than on the correction of misused ones. This exploratory repeated-measures study investigates the potential of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to provide personalized vocabulary practice targeting learner-specific lexical errors in Spanish. Eighty-five L2 and heritage learners across proficiency levels completed 15 individualized exercises generated by a custom GPT-based system from their own writing errors. The tasks varied in goal, format, linguistic complexity, and involvement load (IL). Error recognition and correction were assessed at immediate and delayed post-tests, and mixed-effects models showed that higher exercise performance and task-induced IL predicted better outcomes. Both recognition and correction declined at the delayed post-test, although only recognition did so significantly. Among exercise features, productive, contextualized formats such as text editing, translation, and sentence reconstruction showed strong positive associations with correction, while goals emphasizing paraphrastic flexibility were less favorable. At the learner level, outcomes also varied substantially. Overall, the findings suggest that GenAI can support scalable, individualized, error-driven vocabulary practice. Still, variability across learners and exercises, together with incomplete retention, indicates that personalization alone may not ensure durable learning. Future research should thus examine whether feedback, recycling, and adaptive review improve retention.

Scalable digital conversational agents can reduce access barriers and provide brief, on-demand psychoeducation aligned with stepped‑care models. Secondary aims are to assess acceptability and feasibility, and to explore proximal changes in distress, well-being, psychological flexibility, and knowledge retention. quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction The accelerating production and circulation of digital news have transformed the continuity of public interest. Constant updates, algorithmic visibility, and information abundance shorten the period during which news stories remain prominent. quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support second-language (L2) writers in planning, drafting, revising, and receiving feedback. But the fact that it can write flowing prose does not prove it can reason independently or rely on dependable sources. This critical integrative review explores what source-audited empirical evidence supports about GenAI, L2 English writing, critical thinking, and evidence evaluation. The evidence set comprises 20 bibliographically verified publications. The researcher confirmed that six were tertiary EFL/ESL English academic-writing studies; 13 were closely related L2/EFL writing studies but lacked one strict scope detail in the accessible primary record; and one reading-based critical-thinking study was retained only as contextual evidence. She extracted only facts supported by publisher records, full texts where available, and Crossref metadata. This review is not systematic, and we make no claims about reproducible database-search logs, dual screening, or pooled effect estimation. Across the audited source record, evidence more often concerned immediate assisted revision, feedback, engagement, and process outcomes than independent transfer. Results for critical thinking were mixed and depended on the instructional design and outcome assessed. No study in the evidence set directly assessed citation accuracy, lateral reading, or a similar objective outcome of evidence evaluation. The review thus distinguishes between textual quality, argumentative reasoning, and evidential quality. It argues that GenAI-supported writing pedagogy should require source verification, claim-evidence justification, and AI-free transfer assessment, rather than using polished, AI-assisted text as a proxy for epistemic learning.
